title: Python refuses to sort a list with a missing value; JavaScript sorts it two different ways depending on how you ask
assumption: A missing value (None/null/undefined) in a list of numbers sorts to a predictable, consistent place, or fails loudly the same way everywhere.

input.display: [3, None, 1] in Python; [3, null, 1, undefined, 2] in JavaScript
input.description: A numeric column from a database or API response where some rows legitimately have no value (an unset score, an optional field), sorted for a leaderboard or table.

what_goes_wrong: Python's sorted([3, None, 1]) raises TypeError. JavaScript's default sort compares elements as strings, so null sorts where the string "null" would (after the digits here), while undefined always goes to the very end. With a numeric comparator (a, b) => a - b, null behaves as 0 (Number(null) === 0) and moves to the front, and undefined is still last: the comparator is never called with undefined, so no comparator logic can move it.
why: Python's < raises TypeError when neither operand's comparison method supports the other type, and None has no ordering against int. In JavaScript, the default sort uses ToString (String(null) is "null"), while a subtraction comparator relies on numeric conversion, where Number(null) is 0. undefined never reaches the comparator: the spec's CompareArrayElements returns "undefined goes after" before calling it, so undefined values always end up after every other value (and array holes after those).
fix: Decide explicitly where missing values belong (first, last, or filtered out) and partition or key for that before sorting, rather than letting None/null/undefined flow into the comparison — in JavaScript especially, don't assume your comparator controls where undefined ends up; it doesn't.
